## Why it matters

A late delivery is rarely a surprise to the data: shipping mode, destination market,
product category, order timing and the promised schedule all carry signal. If the risk is
known **when the order is placed**, a company can choose a faster shipping mode, warn the
customer, or reorder stock earlier. This is the business problem behind the project.

## Why Spark

The dataset is large enough, and wide enough (dozens of columns of mixed types), that a
single-machine pandas workflow becomes awkward to repeat and impossible to scale. The
project uses Spark the way it would be used on a real cluster: lazy DataFrame
transformations, a declared schema, and an **MLlib `Pipeline`** whose every step
(indexing, encoding, assembling, scaling, modelling) is fitted on training data only and
can be re-run on new data unchanged.

## The pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[("Raw CSV<br/>DataCo orders")] --> B["Ingest with<br/>explicit schema"]
  B --> C["Clean & dedupe<br/>parse dates"]
  C --> D["Drop leaking<br/>columns"]
  D --> E["Feature engineering<br/>time · market · shipping"]
  E --> F["MLlib Pipeline<br/>StringIndexer → OneHot →<br/>VectorAssembler → Scaler"]
  F --> G["Models<br/>LogReg · RF · GBT"]
  G --> H["CrossValidator<br/>AUC · F1 · recall"]
  H --> I[("Results &<br/>feature importance")]
  classDef done fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#14532D;
  classDef now fill:#FEF3C7,stroke:#D97706,color:#78350F;
  classDef todo fill:#E0E7FF,stroke:#6366F1,color:#1E1B4B;
  class A done; class B now; class C,D,E,F,G,H,I todo;
```

<ol class="steps">
  <li class="done"><b>Problem framing and dataset</b><span>Binary target: late delivery risk. Business metric: recall on late orders, at a controlled false-alarm rate.</span></li>
  <li class="now"><b>Ingestion</b><span>Spark session, explicit schema (no type inference on a large CSV), basic profiling of every column.</span></li>
  <li><b>Cleaning and leakage audit</b><span>Columns only known <i>after</i> shipping (real shipping days, delivery status, shipping date) describe the outcome and must be dropped, or the model learns the answer instead of the risk.</span></li>
  <li><b>Feature engineering</b><span>Order weekday, month and hour; scheduled shipping days; shipping mode; market, region and country; product category; order value and discount.</span></li>
  <li><b>MLlib pipeline</b><span>StringIndexer and OneHotEncoder for categories, VectorAssembler and StandardScaler, fitted on the training split only.</span></li>
  <li><b>Models and tuning</b><span>Logistic regression (baseline), Random Forest and Gradient-Boosted Trees, tuned with CrossValidator on a stratified split.</span></li>
  <li><b>Evaluation</b><span>ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, F1 and recall on late orders; feature importance; error analysis by market and shipping mode.</span></li>
  <li><b>Scaling notes</b><span>Partitioning, caching and run times, to show what changes when the data no longer fits on one machine.</span></li>
</ol>

## The trap this project is designed to avoid

::: {.insight}
**Target leakage.** In this kind of dataset, some columns are recorded after the parcel
has shipped. A model given "actual days for shipping" next to "scheduled days" can reach
near-perfect accuracy by subtracting one from the other, and is useless in practice. The
audit in step 3 decides, column by column, what is genuinely known at order time. Getting
this right matters more than any choice of algorithm.
:::
